sittings.bodyEn: This chapter starts from a year that looked successful and felt empty. Revenue was real, and the days were filled with products he could not defend, a fast hiring spree, a blander brand, and meetings with people he did not want to see. That script came from other people's picture of a proper chief executive. The reason to start was freedom, which can mean mornings with your kids, a remote season, or a product you make because it is cool. Profit is one dial, and it can lose to time, health, or work you can stand behind. The correction was to keep only defensible products, drop toxic relationships, protect the odd details customers liked, and reserve time that was not for the company.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean the business rearranged so the days match the life you actually want.

sittings.bodyEn: In a job you inherit the system. As the owner you design one, and the target is your own happiness. The chapter treats that as permission you give yourself, because it will not arrive from outside. Fear is what keeps the redesign on paper. The other enemy is chaos: kids, a day job, and a full inbox pull at the same hours and the day disappears. A written checklist is how you take the focus back. A steady job that already makes someone happy can be the dream, and this process is for people who want to build the next version themselves.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean the rules and calendar you design around your own happiness.

sittings.bodyEn: Write the dream year as scenes, not a slogan. Include where you live, what you are doing, how you feel, and who you are with. The list in the chapter mixes a revenue picture, a house, trips, a skill, health, and a few experiences that would make the year feel like his. Do not solve the method yet. The point is a vision that excites you, and a written one is harder to abandon when the year turns reactive. Later you will choose which scenes become scheduled goals. If a line is only what you think you should want, leave it off.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a concrete picture of the year, written before you solve how.

sittings.bodyEn: Choose the scenes you are most excited about, and drop any dream you hesitate on. Sort them into work, health, personal life, and travel, and rename the buckets if your life needs different ones. Fewer goals you truly want will beat a heroic list. Continuing a goal from last year is a good sign. You will not finish every line, and the list still works as a priority tool. Aim for goals you can sustain, because one impressive burnout year is less useful than a practice you keep. If a line dies midyear, change it, and plan to review the set about twice a year.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean work, health, personal, and travel, unless your life needs different names.
If they say this, they mean the dream-year scenes you are excited enough to schedule.

sittings.bodyEn: A goal you never see will lose to whatever is loud today. Put the list on the phone lock screen, on a note stuck to the computer, in a file you open each week, on the bathroom mirror, and inside a daily note. Send it to one person who will challenge your excuses, someone you trust to check in. Visibility is the method. When you look at the week, the list should be the standard you measure against. The next step moves those lines onto the calendar, where the hours either match them or they do not.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean the yearly list placed where you see it every day, plus one person who has a copy.

sittings.bodyEn: Everyone has one hundred sixty-eight hours in a week, and the calendar shows what you actually rank first. Give each priority a category and a color, then place the key blocks on the week. In the chapter, work, health, personal, and travel each get a color, and one glance should reveal whether the biggest blocks match the stated goals. If the main goal is barely on the calendar, add it. Front-load that work earlier in the week, when energy is higher. Another organizing method is fine if it does the same job, as long as the hours follow the goals.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a color per life category so one glance shows whether the week matches the goals.

sittings.bodyEn: Spend about fifteen minutes every Sunday looking at the past week and setting the next one. Pick tasks that move a yearly goal, then score last Sunday's list to see whether they did. The review is for accountability and improvement. Rest belongs on the calendar too, and a lazy day is allowed when the important work is already handled. Use that space to ask what you can outsource, stop, or hand to software. Put the blocks that help on repeat, same hours on the same days, so they become automatic and your attention is free for the harder problems.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a short weekly look at promises kept and the tasks that move the yearly goals.
If they say this, they mean the same useful block on the same days until it is a habit.

sittings.bodyEn: You make better choices when someone else can see the promises. Send a weekly note to one peer who will actually reply. Include what you said you would do, what you finished, what slipped, and what next week holds, across the same life buckets. Their job is to mark the small wins and to name the goal you quietly dropped. If they never answer or never challenge a miss, replace them. A silent buddy changes nothing. The chapter has used the same Sunday ritual for years because the reply is the pressure.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean the person who reads your weekly promises and actually answers.
If they say this, they mean people follow through more carefully when someone can see the promise.

sittings.bodyEn: Most of the useful help in this chapter came from people, not from a solo grind. Reach ambitious people before the crowd does, while they still reply and a real relationship is possible. Use three filters: the work impresses you, they are not yet flooded with attention, and you can do something useful for them. The first message is a specific compliment about what they made, with no request attached. A note that asks for a favor in the first line is the wrong shape. A compliment with no expectation is how the conversation starts, and any collaboration comes later. Connect because of where you think they are going.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean someone whose work you respect who will still reply because the crowd has not arrived.

sittings.bodyEn: After a good conversation, send thanks the same day. Include a few highlights you want to remember, the follow-ups you owe, and a request for one or two other people worth meeting. Start the wider net by asking your most impressive friend for a single introduction, and name the topics you care about so the ask is easy to answer. Say there is no pressure if nobody comes to mind. One name is easier to think of than a homework assignment. After you meet that person, thank the original friend and ask the new one for one name of their own.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean asking for a single introduction, with no pressure if none comes to mind.

sittings.bodyEn: The note to a new person has to give them a reason to answer. Say who you are in a short line, what is in it for them, and why you want the meeting. A subject line that names a mutual connection is a strong hook. Mention a specific piece of their work, and only if you actually know it. Offer a concrete time, and add a true detail that shows you can be useful. Leave out those points and expect silence. The sequence is the thank-you, the one referral, and this introduction, repeated.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a short note with who you are, how you can help, why you want to meet, and a specific time.

sittings.bodyEn: The business is supposed to fit the life, so you design the system on purpose. Write a specific dream year, keep the scenes that excite you, and sort them into work, health, personal life, and travel. See that list often, color the week so the hours match it, and use Sunday to score last week and set the next. Repeat the blocks that move the goals, and schedule rest on purpose. A buddy who replies holds the promises, and the wider network grows from early compliments, one referral, and notes that say how you can help. Hesitation, a silent buddy, and someone else's script are the failures this chapter is built to catch.
sittings.prompt: How does this chapter turn a dream year into a week you can keep?
choices: Choose the exciting scenes, put them on a colored calendar, and let a buddy answer the Sunday note
Copy a famous founder's schedule and maximize profit even when you dislike the work
Keep the dream list private so nobody can challenge it
Wait until you feel successful, then design the life
